properties.name: The prose survey extended to the skill corpus — no rot found by sampling, and the method's own flaw was the finding
properties.rationale:
RECORDED AS `documentation` / `record` DELIBERATELY: nothing about the system changed, only what the design knows about its own prose. The tool's own guidance says a normative document that changes what somebody DOES takes a real label instead — this changes nothing anyone does, so it takes the honest small one.

⭐ WHY A NULL RESULT IS WORTH A CHANGE EVENT. The five instances that opened this question made the prose look unreliable. Two surveys across 2,552 sentences found no sixth by sampling, which is the strongest available evidence that the base rate is genuinely low — and that is what decides the repair. An audit of the corpus would be the wrong build: at the observed rate a reader wades through fifty true sentences per false one, and would have found none of the six.

⚠️ WHAT WOULD REFUTE THE CONCLUSION: all six known instances were found on the surfaces users touch most, and both surveys sampled the corpus UNIFORMLY. If rot concentrates where prose is heavily read and heavily edited — which is plausible, since those are the sentences that get outgrown — uniform sampling is the wrong instrument and would report exactly this null. A survey weighted by tool call frequency would test that, and nobody has run one.

SO THE DIRECTION STANDS AND IS UNCHANGED BY THIS: pin the claims that CAN be pinned, on the pattern of `chg:the-replay-contract-is-pinned-by-a-round-trip-not-by-a-field` — a round-trip test rather than a corrected sentence — rather than auditing prose nobody can keep true by reading it.
properties.subject: record
properties.summary:
EXTENDING `fact:the-served-prose-is-mostly-true-and-nothing-checks-any-of-it` to the population it named as unsurveyed: the 25 served skills.

POPULATION: 1,785 sentences. 631 (35%) carry an assertion marker — lower density than tool descriptions (45%), as expected since skills are mostly doctrine. Narrowing to sentences that ALSO name a served tool, which is where a checkable claim about tool behaviour actually lives: 101 sentences (6%), across 23 of 25 skills.

A SAMPLE OF 22 WAS READ. ONE LOOKED LIKE A CLEAN ROT AND WAS NOT.

`retire-from-design` opens its candidate section with *"`consumption_report` names capabilities nothing is recorded as using."* The tool says the opposite where it matters: *"if the design records a consumer for fewer than half of what it built, the list is WITHHELD."* Confirmed in code — `MIN_MODELLED_RATIO = 0.5`, and `if ratio < MIN_MODELLED_RATIO` withholds. On reflow2's own design (8% modelled) the tool names nothing, so the sentence is false exactly where an agent would rely on it.

⭐ **AND THEN THE NEXT PARAGRAPH SAYS IT CORRECTLY**: *"READ ITS REFUSAL AS THE FINDING. On a design where few capabilities have modelled consumers it declines to name them at all."* The section is RIGHT AS A WHOLE. The lead sentence overstates and is qualified three lines later.

**SO THE FINDING IS THE METHOD, NOT THE SENTENCE.** Sentence-level extraction strips the qualifier that makes the prose true — which is the SAME failure dev_storyflow reported in the same week, when their regex for dishonest nodes was 40% wrong because it could not tell a claim from its denial. Their flaw was matching negations; this one is losing context. Both come of scoring prose in units smaller than the argument it makes.

⚠️ THAT BOUND APPLIES BACKWARDS to the tool-description survey too, though more weakly: a tool description is one blob with no paragraph structure, so a qualifier is likelier to sit in the same sentence — but the 80% "makes a checkable claim" figure was also judged sentence by sentence and should be read with this in mind.

RESULT ACROSS BOTH POPULATIONS: **zero rotted claims found by sampling.** 5 of 5 verified true in tool descriptions; 22 read in skills with one candidate refuted by its own context. All six known-false instances to date were found by USERS hitting them, never by inspection.
